name: Nineveh
info: Nineveh was an ancient city of Upper Mesopotamia on the eastern bank of the Tigris, in the present-day city of Mosul in northern Iraq, founded as early as 6000 BCE and the capital of the Neo-Assyrian Empire.

facts.founded: As early as 6000 BCE, during the late Neolithic period, as a farming village; in the Hebrew Bible (Genesis 10:11) the city is built by Ashur, though some modern translations make Nimrod its founder.
facts.where: On the eastern bank of the Tigris at its junction with the Khosr River, on a level part of the plain of Upper Mesopotamia, in the present-day city of Mosul in northern Iraq.
facts.known: Capital and largest city of the Neo-Assyrian Empire; Sennacherib's South West Palace; the library of Ashurbanipal; the sack of 612 BCE; the prophet Jonah in the Hebrew Bible and the Quran; the Assyrian sculptures in museums around the world
facts.today: The ruins lie across the river from the historical centre of Mosul, and the name Nineveh is also used for the half of Mosul on the eastern bank and for the Nineveh Governorate.

t: Nineveh grew from a farming village of the 6th millennium BCE into a proto-city, a trade colony of Uruk and a provincial town of Assyria before Sennacherib made it a truly influential city around 700 BCE.

It was the capital and largest city of the Neo-Assyrian Empire until a coalition of former subject peoples besieged and sacked it in 612 BCE, after which it was never again a political or administrative centre.

A settlement survived under the Persians, Seleucids, Parthians and Sasanians and became a bishopric of the Church of the East, but it was eclipsed by Mosul and mostly abandoned by the 14th century CE.
dyk: Sennacherib's South West Palace had at least 80 rooms, and the foundation under it was made of roughly 2,680,000 cubic metres of brick, about 160 million bricks.
ev: Nineveh is founded as a farming village in the late Neolithic period
Ashur-uballit I reclaims the city from Mitanni and founds the Middle Assyrian Empire
Sennacherib lays out new streets and squares and builds the South West Palace
A coalition of Babylonians, Medes and Scythians sacks and razes the city
Nineveh is a bishopric of the Church of the East
The Arabs conquer the area and build a mosque on the west bank
Benjamin of Tudela visits the site

sections.origins:
Nineveh stood on the eastern bank of the Tigris at its junction with the Khosr River, on a level part of the plain of Upper Mesopotamia. The site lies in the present-day city of Mosul in northern Iraq. The English name comes from the Latin Nīnevē and the Greek Nineuḗ, under the influence of the Biblical Hebrew Nīnəweh, from the Akkadian Ninua. The ruins lie within an area of 750 hectares circumscribed by a fortification wall 12 kilometres long, and the two main mounds inside it are Tell Kuyunjiq and Tell Nabī Yūnus.

The city was founded as early as 6000 BCE, in the late Neolithic period. Deep soundings reached soil layers from early in the Hassuna culture, and a deep sounding at Kuyunjiq by Max Mallowan showed habitation in the 6th millennium BCE. Nineveh was a typical farming village in the Halaf period, and in 5000 BCE it became an Ubaid village. It was one of the few Ubaid villages of Upper Mesopotamia that became a proto-city, and between 4500 and 4000 BCE it grew to 40 hectares. In the Uruk period it was a trade colony of Uruk, because it was the highest navigable point on the Tigris. The Hebrew Bible first mentions it in Genesis 10:11: "Ashur left that land, and built Nineveh". Some modern English translations read Ashur as the country Assyria rather than a person, which makes Nimrod the founder.
sections.growth:
After the Uruk period the regional influence of Nineveh became particularly pronounced. The Ninevite 5 period (3000/2900 to 2600/2500 BCE) takes its name from the characteristic pottery found widely throughout Upper Mesopotamia. In the early 2nd millennium BCE the city became a centre of worship of Ishtar, and Assyrian monarchs built extensively there in the late 3rd and 2nd millennia BCE, apparently from the starting point of an Assyrian provincial town. Inscriptions of the Middle Assyrian kings Shalmaneser I and Tiglath-Pileser I have been found on the high city.

From the time of Ashurnasirpal II, who ruled from 883 to 859 BCE, there was considerable architectural expansion. Later kings maintained and founded palaces and temples to Sîn, Ashur, Nergal, Shamash, Ninurta, Ishtar, Tammuz, Nisroch and Nabu. It was Sennacherib who made Nineveh a truly influential city around 700 BCE. He laid out new streets and squares and built the South West Palace, which had at least 80 rooms and measured about 503 by 242 metres. At this time the city covered about 7 square kilometres and fifteen great gates penetrated its walls. Eighteen canals brought water from the hills, and a stone aqueduct built by Sennacherib has been found at Jerwan, about 65 kilometres away. The enclosed area held more than 100,000 inhabitants, perhaps closer to 150,000, about twice as many as Babylon at the time.
sections.rulers:
In the late 3rd millennium BCE Nineveh was part of the Akkadian Empire, though there was minimal official Akkadian presence there, unlike at Assur. In the early 2nd millennium BCE it became part of the Kingdom of Upper Mesopotamia under Shamshi-Adad I, an Amorite ruler of Ekallatum who reigned from about 1809 to 1775 BCE. A statue of Ishtar was sent from the city to the pharaoh Amenhotep III of Egypt in the 14th century BCE by order of Tushratta of Mitanni, and Nineveh was for half a century a vassal of Mitanni. Ashur-uballit I reclaimed it in 1365 BCE while overthrowing the Mitanni Empire and creating the Middle Assyrian Empire.

Under the Neo-Assyrian Empire Nineveh was the capital and largest city, and Sennacherib, Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal were among the kings who built there. After 612 BCE it is not clear whether the city came under the Medes or the Neo-Babylonian Empire. The Cyrus Cylinder of 539 or 538 BCE possibly records that Cyrus the Great restored the temple of Ishtar at Nineveh, though the reading is disputed. The city was actively resettled under the Seleucid Empire, and under the Parthians it had a municipal mint that coined in bronze. According to Tacitus, Meherdates, a claimant to the Parthian throne with Roman support, took Nineveh in 50 CE. Under the Sasanian Empire it was not an administrative centre. The Arabs conquered it in 641.
sections.life:
Nineveh was a city of temples and palaces. Its kings built temples to many gods, and the city was long a centre of the worship of Ishtar. Sennacherib's palace was entered through doorways flanked by colossal winged lions or bulls with human heads, the lamassu, which weighed up to 30,000 kilograms and were carried 50 kilometres from quarries at Balatai. The palace walls were lined with sculpture, and reliefs documented every step of the building work, including the transport of a colossal statue on a barge. The sculpted walls also showed battle scenes, impalings and Sennacherib's men parading the spoils of war before him. A large number of cuneiform tablets was found in the palace, and the palace of Ashurbanipal held a famous library of 22,000 cuneiform clay tablets.

The city was ringed by a wall about 6 metres of stone topped by about 10 metres of mudbrick, 15 metres thick, with stone towers about every 18 metres. Its gates took their names from gods, among them the Nergal, Adad and Shamash Gates, and the Mashki Gate may have been used to take livestock to water from the Tigris. After 612 BCE the temple of Nabu was repaired and Sennacherib's palace stayed in use. Later cults mixed local and Greek practice, and a statue of Hermes and a Greek inscription at a shrine of the Sebitti have been found. By the 2nd century CE there were Christians in the city, and Christian monasteries were built around 570 and 595.
sections.crises:
The greatness of Nineveh was short-lived. Around 627 BCE, after the death of Ashurbanipal, the last great king, the Neo-Assyrian Empire began to unravel through civil wars between rival claimants for the throne. In 616 BCE Assyria was attacked by its former vassals, the Chaldeans, Babylonians, Medes and Scythians, and about then Kalhu was sacked. The allied forces eventually reached Nineveh, which they besieged and sacked in 612 BCE after bitter house-to-house fighting, and the city was then razed. Most of the people who could not escape to the last Assyrian strongholds in the north and west were either massacred or deported into the countryside, where they founded new settlements. Archaeologists found many unburied skeletons at the site, and human remains from the final battle lay in the passage of the Halzi Gate. The Assyrian Empire ended by 605 BCE.

The Babylonian Chronicle says that Nineveh was "turned into mounds and heaps", but this is literary hyperbole, and the city was not completely abandoned. Yet to the Greek historians Ctesias and Herodotus around 400 BCE it was a thing of the past, and Xenophon described it as abandoned. In 627 CE it was the site of the Battle of Nineveh between the Eastern Roman Empire and the Sasanians. Under the Umayyads Mosul eclipsed Nineveh, which was reduced to a Christian suburb with limited new construction. By the 13th century it was mostly ruins and was absorbed into Mosul, and it was mostly abandoned by the 14th century after the massacres and dispersal of Assyrian Christians by Timur.
sections.legacy:
In the Hebrew Bible Nineveh is the object of prophecy. The Book of Nahum is almost wholly taken up with denunciations of it, and Zephaniah also foretells its destruction. The Book of Jonah describes it as an exceedingly great city of three days' journey in breadth, with a population of more than 120,000, whose people fasted and repented when Jonah preached to them. According to the Hebrew Bible and the Quran Jonah was a prophet who preached to Nineveh. A church was converted into a Muslim shrine to Jonah on the mound of Nabī Yūnus, which drew pilgrims until it was destroyed by ISIL in 2014. Several Eastern churches keep a fast called Ba'uta d-Ninwe, Nineveh's Prayer.

The location of Nineveh was known to some continuously through the Middle Ages, and Benjamin of Tudela visited it in 1170. Austen Henry Layard rediscovered the palace of Sennacherib in 1849, and large numbers of Assyrian sculptures and other artefacts have since been excavated and are now in museums around the world. Some scholars, among them Stephanie Dalley, hold that the garden Sennacherib built beside his palace was the original Hanging Gardens of Babylon. The ruins across the river from the historical centre of Mosul are partly overlaid by the eastern suburbs of Mosul, and an archaeological park was opened at Kuyunjiq in 2023.

summary: Nineveh was a city of Upper Mesopotamia on the eastern bank of the Tigris, founded as early as 6000 BCE. It was the capital and largest city of the Neo-Assyrian Empire until its sack in 612 BCE, and was mostly abandoned by the 14th century CE. Its ruins lie in Mosul.
references: John Malcolm Russell, Sennacherib's "Palace without Rival" at Nineveh (University Of Chicago Press, 1992)
Richard David Barnett, Sculptures from the north palace of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh (668-627 B.C.) (British Museum Publications Ltd, 1976)

END: the article gives no single end year. It says Nineveh was mostly ruins by the 13th century and mostly abandoned by the 14th century CE; I used c. 1300 with endCirca true. The city was never again a political centre after 612 BCE, which could also be read as its end as a city.
START: 6000 BCE is the article's 'as early as 6000 BC'; circa true.

WALL: the article gives 'about 6 metres' of stone and 'about 10 metres high and 15 metres thick' mudbrick, dated about 700 BCE; I wrote 'about 6 metres of stone topped by about 10 metres of mudbrick, 15 metres thick'.
POPULATION: the article gives 'more than 100,000 (maybe closer to 150,000)'; kept as given. The Jonah figure 'more than 120,000' is attributed to the Book of Jonah.
The article says both 'it was razed' and that the city was not completely abandoned after 612 BCE; both kept, with the Babylonian Chronicle's phrase called hyperbole as the article does.
The Cyrus Cylinder reading is disputed in the article; hedged.

Left out: Ninevite 5 pottery comparisons, copper smelting at Tell Arpachiyah and Tepe Gawra, the Sennacherib inscriptions on Babylon and Lachish (grim boasts), the Kuyunjiq/Nebi Yunus gate-by-gate archaeology of the 2010s, the destruction of the Mosul Museum, the Mosul Dam, and the poems and games in popular culture. The ISIL destruction of the shrine is mentioned once in legacy.
The 1170 visit of Benjamin of Tudela is in the article's intro; used as an event though it is in the article before the Name section, not in the History.

The article says the Battle of Nineveh of 627 was between the Eastern Roman Empire and the Sasanians; 'In 641 conquered by the Arabs, who built a mosque on the west bank and turned it into an administrative centre' refers to the settlement later called Mosul; I wrote that the Arabs conquered it in 641 and, in the event line, that they built a mosque on the west bank.
ARTICLE ODDITY: the article says 'Nineveh IV became a trade colony of Uruk'; 'Nineveh IV' not reproduced.
